analysis.one_liner: Taxes big oil companies when crude prices spike above 2025 levels and rebates the money to taxpayers.
analysis.headline: The bill has 13 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents, and has sat in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote since it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill puts a 50% excise tax on each barrel of crude oil extracted in or imported into the United States by large oil companies — those moving at least 300,000 barrels a day — whenever the average quarterly price of Brent crude exceeds its 2025 average. All the money collected goes into a dedicated fund and is paid back to individual taxpayers as a 'gasoline price rebate,' with higher payments for joint filers and the rebate phasing out for incomes above $75,000 ($150,000 for couples). It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Middle- and lower-income households, who receive the full rebate; it phases out at 5 cents per dollar of income above $75,000 for singles and $150,000 for joint filers, so wealthier households get little or nothing [S2]. Rebates are refundable, meaning people who owe little or no federal income tax still get paid [S2]. Joint filers get 150% of the standard rebate [S2].

how_it_helps.text: When crude prices spike above the 2025 average, large oil companies pay a 50% excise tax on the excess price per barrel, capturing part of the windfall for the public [S2].
The entire tax is deposited in a 'Protect Consumers from Gas Hikes Fund' and paid out to eligible individuals as a gasoline price rebate, determined quarterly based on the revenues collected [S2].
The rebate is fully refundable, phases out only above $75,000 of income ($150,000 for joint returns), and the Treasury must run an outreach program so eligible taxpayers know to claim it [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large oil companies — those extracting or importing more than 300,000 barrels of crude per day — pay the excise tax. To the extent companies raise pump prices or cut back output to offset the tax, drivers could pay part of it at the gas station, particularly when prices are already spiking [S2].

drawbacks.text: An excise tax on crude is likely to be partly passed through to consumers, so drivers could face higher pump prices at the very moments the tax applies — when oil prices are already elevated [S2].

The tax rises with any price above the 2025 Brent average, which includes normal inflation and global supply shocks unrelated to oil company profits; a genuine crisis-driven price spike would be taxed the same as a margin windfall [S2].

Only companies above a 300,000 barrel-per-day threshold pay, so smaller producers face no tax, and the rebate depends on prices actually exceeding the 2025 baseline — in a year of normal or falling prices, no revenue and no rebates flow [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If prices spike, the bill shifts a share of windfall revenue from large oil companies to lower- and middle-income households, which is a real transfer toward working people. But it is a spike-triggered tax, not a permanent one: the honest cost is that some of the tax may show up in pump prices during a spike, and the design — pegged to a 2025 price floor and a size threshold — is a blunt instrument that taxes global supply shocks as well as profit margins.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no action on it; it has not received a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the Big Oil Windfall Profits Tax Act on March 17, 2026, with 12 Democratic cosponsors [S2].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance, where its complete action history ends [S4].
All 13 cosponsors are Democrats or independents; no Republican has signed on [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, large oil companies benefit from the status quo: the bill sits in committee with no scheduled action, so no new tax on their windfall profits has been enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big oil, since the bill has not advanced

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors are Democrats or independents; no Republican support appears in the record, and the bill has not reached a floor vote where party breakdowns could be measured.

industries.note: Companies moving more than 300,000 barrels of crude per day would pay a 50% excise tax on the amount by which Brent prices exceed their 2025 average, cutting into windfall revenue when prices spike. Their interest in blocking the bill runs directly against the rebate benefits households would receive from the fund.

Producers under the 300,000 barrel-per-day threshold owe no tax, but a tax on the largest players covering US-extracted and imported crude could still affect market prices and demand for crude from all producers.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has been referred to the Senate Finance Committee with no Republican cosponsors and no committee action scheduled. Windfall profits tax proposals from previous Congresses similarly never received a markup or floor vote. Unless the committee schedules action or oil-price politics changes the calculus, the most likely path is that the bill sits without a vote through the end of the 119th Congress.
